outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the survey paper. It will outline the rapid evolution of LLM security threats from 2023 to 2026, covering data poisoning, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and hallucinations. It will highlight the transition from static, unimodal vulnerabilities to dynamic, multimodal, and agentic adversarial arms races, summarizing the state-of-the-art in both offensive techniques and defensive mitigations.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: Establish the motivation and scope of the survey, contextualizing the rapid deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) against the escalating landscape of security vulnerabilities. Outline the temporal evolution from 2023 to 2026, noting the shift from isolated, domain-specific vulnerabilities to a highly sophisticated, co-evolutionary adversarial arms race. Summarize the core contributions of this survey: a comprehensive systematization of training-time threats (poisoning), inference-time threats (adversarial attacks, prompt injection), model reliability issues (hallucinations), and the corresponding defensive paradigms. Provide a roadmap for the subsequent sections.

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: Provide the foundational concepts necessary for understanding LLM security. Define core terminology strictly, including Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (direct vs. indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO, SFT), and Red Teaming. Briefly overview standard LLM and MLLM architectures (e.g., Transformers, MoE) and how they process inputs, without over-claiming specific attack papers as architectural sources. Establish the threat model taxonomy, distinguishing between white-box (full gradient/weight access) and black-box (query-only) adversary capabilities, and differentiate between training-time and inference-time threat vectors.

outline.title: 3. Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: Detail the 2024-2025 evolution of data and model poisoning within foundation models. Discuss the foundational 2024 benchmarking of generative backdoors in open-source models like LLaMA-2, Mistral, and GPT-J, explicitly referencing the frameworks provided by [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking] and [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Explain how these early studies demonstrated the inadequacy of traditional defenses against generative backdoor threats. Transition to the late 2024/2025 shift where attacks expanded beyond unimodal text generation into complex multimodal environments and embodied AI. Highlight the exploitation of alignment and retrieval mechanisms, specifically detailing vulnerabilities within the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipeline.

outline.title: 4. Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks
outline.description: Analyze the 2024-2026 trajectory of adversarial attacks on LLMs and MLLMs. Highlight the 2024 focus on baseline vulnerabilities in high-stakes, specialized domains, specifically discussing how standard models were manipulated when processing sensitive healthcare datasets like MIMIC-III [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Describe the transition from these initial domain-specific exploits to a sophisticated, multi-faceted arms race characterized by advanced offensive weaponization. Discuss the mechanics of adversarial suffixes, token manipulation, and how attackers exploit the high-dimensional continuous spaces of LLM embeddings to force unintended behaviors.

outline.title: 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: Examine the 2025-2026 shift from static, rule-based defenses to automated adversarial arms races in prompt injection and jailbreaking. Detail offensive advancements using adaptive optimization techniques. Specifically, discuss the application of modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms that achieved alarming Attack Success Rates (ASR) ranging from 50% to 71% against state-of-the-art LLM agents, referencing [Zhan_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_LLM, Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Explore the bifurcation of this trend into the pursuit of extreme computational efficiency for attackers and the exploitation of agentic environments.

outline.title: 6. Model Reliability and Factual Consistency: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: Trace the 2023-2026 evolution of hallucination detection and mitigation. Cover the 2023 era of establishing baseline detection methodologies, focusing on zero-shot inference-time methods and the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm. Specifically highlight the introduction of ChainPoll [Friel_2023_LLM], detailing how it utilized LLM-based polling and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to drastically reduce inference costs while outperforming competitors. Transition to the 2024 conceptual maturation, where the field moved away from treating all non-factual generations as binary errors, shifting toward highly optimized, mechanistically informed, and conceptually nuanced frameworks for evaluating factual consistency.

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: Synthesize holistic defense strategies across the identified threat vectors. Contrast early 2024 'patchwork' defenses, such as external stateful detection and prompt-level manipulations. Specifically detail contrastive prompt tuning as a mechanism to detect query-based black-box attacks, noting its 99% detection rate [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. Discuss the evolution toward dynamic, ensemble-based defensive systems in 2025-2026 designed to counter automated optimization attacks (e.g., modified GCG). Cover architectural interventions, perplexity filters, robust alignment techniques, and the integration of security directly into the model's training and retrieval pipelines.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: Critically evaluate testing methodologies, benchmarks, datasets, and metrics across all threat categories (Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Prompt Injection, Hallucinations). Discuss the standardization of Attack Success Rate (ASR) for jailbreaks and prompt injections. Review the datasets used for evaluating domain-specific vulnerabilities (e.g., MIMIC-III for healthcare) and the benchmarks for generative backdoors. Analyze the metrics used for hallucination detection, contrasting exact match with LLM-evaluated semantic equivalence. Address the challenges of evaluating dynamic, agentic attacks (e.g., MCTS fuzzing) and the necessity for reproducible, standardized red-teaming frameworks.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: Identify critical gaps and limitations in the current LLM security landscape. Discuss the fundamental tension between model utility (alignment) and security (robustness). Address the open challenges in defending against adaptive, co-evolutionary attacks in multi-agent systems. Highlight the lack of theoretical guarantees for empirical defenses and the difficulties in scaling robust training methods to trillion-parameter models. Propose future research directions, including the need for mechanistically interpretable security, cross-modal defense generalization, and standardized regulatory compliance testing.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: Provide a final synthesis of the survey's findings. Reiterate the rapid paradigm shift from static, unimodal vulnerabilities to dynamic, automated adversarial arms races. Offer practical recommendations for practitioners deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments, emphasizing the necessity of defense-in-depth strategies that combine robust alignment, continuous red-teaming, and dynamic inference-time monitoring.

background_and_preliminaries.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
background_and_preliminaries.text:
# 2. Background and Preliminaries

To establish a solid foundation for understanding the landscape of adversarial attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs), this section introduces the core concepts, definitions, and frameworks that underpin this research area. We begin by defining the essential terminology used throughout the literature. Next, we formalize the threat models that characterize the attacker's objectives and capabilities. We then discuss safety alignment techniques, which represent the primary defense mechanisms employed by model developers, and explain why they remain vulnerable. Finally, we categorize attacks based on the adversary's level of access, distinguishing between white-box and black-box settings.

## 2.1 Terminology

The study of adversarial robustness in LLMs has developed a specialized lexicon. Understanding these terms is crucial for navigating the literature and comprehending the nuances of different attack and defense strategies.

- **Large Language Models (LLMs):** Foundation models based on the Transformer architecture, pre-trained on massive text corpora to predict the next token. Through scaling laws, these models exhibit emergent abilities, including complex reasoning, instruction following, and in-context learning.
- **Adversarial Attack:** In the context of machine learning, an adversarial attack involves crafting inputs specifically designed to cause a model to produce an incorrect, unintended, or harmful output. For LLMs, this typically manifests as manipulating the input prompt to bypass safety restrictions, degrade performance, or alter the model's intended behavior.
- **Jailbreak:** A jailbreak is a specific, highly prevalent type of adversarial attack targeting aligned LLMs. The goal of a jailbreak is to circumvent the model's built-in safety filters and ethical guidelines, compelling it to generate restricted content, such as hate speech, instructions for illegal acts, or toxic text. Jailbreaks often employ role-playing, hypothetical scenarios, or complex logical constructs to deceive the model.
- **Red Teaming:** Borrowed from cybersecurity, red teaming refers to the systematic and rigorous testing of an AI system to identify vulnerabilities, biases, and failure modes before deployment. Internal red-teaming pipelines are increasingly used by developers to curate prompts that expose unsafe model behaviors, which are subsequently used to improve model robustness and alignment [Liu_2025_Purpcode].
- **Adversarial Prompt / Suffix:** The specific string of text (often seemingly nonsensical or carefully engineered) appended to or wrapped around a malicious request to form the attack. In discrete text spaces, these prompts must often adhere to syntactic and semantic constraints, especially in specialized domains like code generation where functional equivalence and grammatical correctness must be preserved [Yin_2025_LLM].

## 2.2 Threat Models

A well-defined threat model is essential for evaluating the severity of an attack and the efficacy of a defense. It specifies the attacker's goals, their knowledge of the target system, and the capabilities at their disposal.

**Attacker Goals:** The primary objective of an adversary targeting an LLM generally falls into one of several categories:
1. **Safety Bypass (Jailbreaking):** Eliciting harmful, toxic, or restricted information that the model is explicitly trained to refuse.
2. **Malicious Code Generation:** Tricking the model into generating functionally correct but insecure code. This includes code with missing input validation when handling external data, unsafe memory management in low-level languages, or incomplete authentication logic [Thang_2026_LLM].
3. **Data Extraction:** Forcing the model to memorize and regurgitate sensitive, copyrighted, or private information present in its training data.
4. **Misinformation and Hallucination:** Manipulating the model to produce plausible but factually incorrect information, which can be weaponized for propaganda, phishing, or social engineering.

**Attacker Capabilities:** The attacker's capabilities dictate how they can interact with the model. In the most common scenario, the attacker acts as a standard user interacting with the LLM via an API or a chat interface. They can submit arbitrary text prompts and observe the model's textual responses. More sophisticated attackers might have the ability to automate thousands of queries, analyze the timing of responses, or, in some cases, access the probability distributions (logits) of the generated tokens. The threat model must also consider whether the attacker can modify the system prompt (e.g., in prompt injection attacks) or if they are strictly restricted to user-level input.

## 2.3 Safety Alignment

To mitigate the risks associated with deploying powerful LLMs, developers employ a process known as safety alignment. Alignment aims to ensure that the model's behavior conforms to human values, ethical guidelines, and safety policies, making the model both helpful and harmless.

The alignment process typically occurs post-training and involves several stages:
- **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT):** The pre-trained model is fine-tuned on a curated dataset of high-quality, human-written instructions and safe responses. This teaches the model the desired format of interaction and basic safety rules. However, SFT largely depends on expensive, high-quality response collections and may not generalize well to unseen adversarial inputs or complex reasoning tasks [Liu_2025_Purpcode].
- **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF):** This technique involves training a separate reward model based on human preference data (e.g., humans ranking which of two model responses is safer or more helpful). The LLM's policy is then optimized using reinforcement learning algorithms to maximize the expected reward, effectively steering the model away from generating harmful content [Liu_2025_Purpcode].
- **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO):** An increasingly popular alternative to RLHF, DPO bypasses the need for a separate reward model by directly optimizing the LLM's policy to increase the likelihood of preferred responses and decrease the likelihood of rejected responses, simplifying the alignment pipeline.

Despite these sophisticated alignment techniques, LLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This vulnerability stems from the fundamental tension between helpfulness and harmlessness. Models are trained to follow user instructions closely; adversarial attacks exploit this by framing harmful requests within complex, seemingly benign instructions that the model prioritizes over its safety training. Furthermore, alignment is often superficial, teaching the model to recognize specific patterns of harmful requests rather than instilling robust, generalizable safety reasoning. Consequently, novel jailbreaks can easily bypass these defenses, highlighting the need for more advanced alignment approaches that incorporate explicit safety reasoning [Liu_2025_Purpcode].

## 2.4 White-box vs. Black-box Attacks

Adversarial attacks are broadly categorized based on the adversary's level of access to the target model's internal workings. This distinction fundamentally shapes the techniques available to the attacker and the realism of the threat.

**White-box Attacks:**
In a white-box setting, the adversary has full, unrestricted access to the target model. This includes knowledge of the model's architecture, its training data, and, crucially, its parameters (weights and biases) [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. This level of access allows the attacker to compute adversarial gradients directly. By backpropagating the loss from a target harmful output back to the input tokens, the attacker can identify exactly how to perturb the input to achieve their goal. 

Techniques like the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) leverage this gradient information to iteratively search for adversarial suffixes that reliably trigger jailbreaks. While white-box attacks are highly effective and provide theoretical upper bounds on model vulnerability, they are often unrealistic for attacking proprietary, commercial LLMs (e.g., GPT-4, Claude 3) which are kept strictly behind APIs and do not expose their weights.

**Black-box Attacks:**
In a black-box setting, the adversary has no knowledge of the model's internal parameters or architecture. They can only interact with the target model by submitting inputs (queries) and observing the outputs (returns) [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. The outputs may be limited to the final generated text (hard-label black-box) or may include the probability scores of the generated tokens (soft-label black-box).

Because direct gradient computation is impossible, black-box attackers must rely on alternative strategies:
- **Query-based Optimization:** The attacker systematically queries the target model, using heuristic search algorithms (like genetic algorithms or particle swarm optimization) to iteratively refine the prompt based on the model's responses. This approach can be query-intensive and may be thwarted by rate limits, API costs, or query detection mechanisms [Wang_2024_Advqdet].
- **Transfer-based Attacks:** The attacker leverages a surrogate white-box model (e.g., an open-source model like Llama 3) to generate adversarial examples using gradient-based methods. They then transfer these attacks to the target black-box model, relying on the phenomenon that adversarial examples often transfer across different models trained on similar data distributions.
- **Manual and Automated Prompt Engineering:** Attackers use intuition, psychological manipulation (e.g., role-playing), or automated LLM-assisted tools to craft prompts that exploit the target model's semantic understanding without relying on mathematical optimization.

Unlike continuous-space perturbations in computer vision, text-based adversarial attacks operate in discrete spaces. Whether in a white-box or black-box setting, the attacker must navigate the challenge of finding discrete token combinations that achieve the adversarial goal. This introduces unique technical challenges absent in other domains, as the adversarial transformations must often preserve functional equivalence and grammatical correctness to be effective [Yin_2025_LLM].

introduction.title: 1. Introduction
introduction.text:
# 1. Introduction

The emergence of artificial intelligence has driven a significant transformation in natural language processing, with large language models (LLMs) enabling unprecedented advances in language comprehension and generation [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. These models have consistently outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods across various benchmarking tasks [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Consequently, LLMs and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are being rapidly integrated into diverse sectors, ranging from automated customer support and content creation to highly specialized domains such as healthcare and education [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking, Yang_2024_Adversarial, Liu_2025_Aegis]. Furthermore, the strong planning and reasoning capabilities of LLMs have fostered the development of agent-based systems that interact with complex environments using external tools [Wang_2025_LLM]. However, this extensive integration carries consequential societal ramifications, as the susceptibility of these models to malicious manipulation poses a significant risk to their integrity and reliability [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking, Yang_2024_Adversarial].

The landscape of LLM safety research has undergone a rapid temporal evolution. Between 2020 and 2026, the field progressed through distinct phases, beginning with a foundation era focused on establishing safety alignment through techniques like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [Wang_2026_LLM]. This was quickly followed by a period of rapid development characterized by the proliferation of novel benchmarks, sophisticated attack vectors, and corresponding defensive mechanisms [Wang_2026_LLM]. During this time, the threat model shifted from isolated, domain-specific vulnerabilities to a highly sophisticated, co-evolutionary adversarial arms race [Liu_2025_Aegis]. As attackers continuously refine their adversarial strategies, defenders are forced to adapt in response, highlighting the necessity for automated, co-evolutionary frameworks to discover robust defenses [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Looking forward, the research trajectory is increasingly directed toward achieving certified robustness to guarantee model security in adversarial environments [Wang_2026_LLM].

The contemporary LLM security threat landscape encompasses vulnerabilities across both the training and inference phases. During pre-training and fine-tuning, models are susceptible to data poisoning, where adversaries manipulate training data to embed malicious behaviors [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Recent work has demonstrated the feasibility of indirect data poisoning, which allows attackers to covertly enforce arbitrary hidden behaviors into a model without degrading its performance on standard benchmarks [Bouaziz_2025_Winter]. At inference time, LLMs face severe threats from adversarial attacks and jailbreaks designed to bypass safety alignment and elicit prohibited outputs [Wang_2026_LLM]. Prompt injection attacks exploit the semantic and contextual flexibility of natural language to manipulate models into producing unintended or harmful responses [Liu_2025_Aegis]. These vulnerabilities extend to specialized applications; for instance, LLM-as-a-judge systems, which are increasingly used to evaluate text quality and code correctness, have proven highly susceptible to sophisticated prompt injections [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. 

Furthermore, the integration of external tools in LLM agents has expanded the attack surface, introducing critical risks such as indirect prompt injection (IPI) [Wang_2025_LLM]. In these scenarios, contextual information retrieved from external sources is manipulated to compromise the agent, and recent evaluations demonstrate that adaptive attacks can consistently bypass existing IPI defenses with high success rates [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Multimodal architectures also remain vulnerable to transferable adversarial examples, where adversaries align global and local features to execute targeted attacks across different, often closed-source, model families [Jia_2025_Adversarial].

Beyond adversarial exploitation, model reliability remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Hallucinations—defined as the generation of inaccurate or unmotivated claims—are widely recognized as a primary ethical and safety pitfall [Sui_2024_Confabulation, Friel_2023_LLM]. Despite extensive mitigation efforts, hallucinations persist and present an imminent risk to model trustworthiness, carrying severe epistemic consequences in truth-sensitive domains such as law, medicine, finance, and science [Sui_2024_Confabulation]. Consequently, the development of robust, automated metrics for hallucination detection is imperative [Friel_2023_LLM, Shelmanov_2025_LLM]. Recent methodologies have proposed metrics such as Adherence, which measures an LLM's reasoning abilities within provided documents for Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) workflows, and Correctness, which captures general logical mistakes [Friel_2023_LLM].

To address these escalating challenges, this survey provides a comprehensive examination of the attacks targeting LLMs, elucidating their underlying mechanisms, potential consequences, and the fast-evolving threat landscape [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The core contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we present a novel taxonomy that categorizes the LLM attack literature, providing a structured systematization of training-time threats, inference-time vulnerabilities, and reliability issues [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Second, we critically evaluate the effectiveness of existing attack methodologies, including adaptive attacks that have successfully bypassed current safeguard systems [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Third, we review the corresponding defensive paradigms, encompassing data filtering, guardrails, robust training techniques, adversarial co-training, and prompt-based defenses [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking, Liu_2025_Aegis, Wang_2026_LLM]. We also examine the nuances of deploying these defenses, such as the complex interactions between few-shot demonstrations and system prompt strategies, which can inadvertently degrade safety if not carefully managed [Wang_2026_LLM]. Additionally, we highlight emerging lightweight solutions, such as real-time self-tuning moderator frameworks, that defend against jailbreaks without the significant barriers of traditional fine-tuning [Zhang_2025_Real]. 

The remainder of this survey is structured as follows: Section 2 details training-time vulnerabilities such as data poisoning; Section 3 explores inference-time threats, including adversarial attacks and prompt injections; Section 4 examines model reliability and hallucination mitigation; and Section 5 discusses comprehensive defense strategies and future directions toward certified robustness.

testing_methodologies_and_evaluation.text:
## 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation

The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has necessitated the development of rigorous, standardized testing methodologies to evaluate their security posture. Historically, the evaluation of LLM vulnerabilities relied on ad-hoc testing and static datasets, which often proved insufficient for practical deployment in real-world scenarios [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Consequently, the establishment of scalable, near-real-time evaluation infrastructures has emerged as a crucial requirement for ensuring ethical reliability and factual performance [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. This section critically evaluates the testing methodologies, benchmarks, datasets, and metrics across four primary threat categories: Data and Model Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Prompt Injection, and LLM Hallucinations. 

### 7.1 Summary of Evaluation Frameworks

To provide a structured overview of the current evaluation landscape, Table 1 summarizes the prominent benchmarks, metrics, and frameworks utilized across different LLM security domains.

| Threat Category | Prominent Benchmarks & Datasets | Standard Evaluation Metrics | Tools & Frameworks | Representative Literature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Data & Model Poisoning** | Stanford Alpaca, AdvBench, ToxiGen, BOLD, GSM8K, MATH | Clean Loss, Backdoor Loss | BackdoorLLM | [Li_2024_Backdoorllm] |
| **Adversarial Attacks** | HarmBench, CyberSecEval, CodeLM-Sec, EvalPlus | Attack Success Rate (ASR) | MART, HARM, RedAgent | [Wang_2026_LLM], [Liu_2025_Purpcode] |
| **Prompt Injection** | AgentDojo, VWA-adv, Mirror Holdout | ASR, F1 Score, Precision, Recall | AGENTVIGIL, AEGIS, RTST | [Wang_2025_LLM], [Corll_2026_Mirror], [Zhang_2025_Real], [Liu_2025_Aegis] |
| **LLM Hallucinations** | RealHall, HaluEval, HalluQA, Amazon Reviews | AUROC, NLI Entailment, Cross-persona Cosine Similarity | ChainPoll, ConsistencyAI, SelfCheckGPT | [Friel_2023_LLM], [Gu_2024_Anah], [Banyas_2025_LLMs], [Kabongo_2025_Factual] |

### 7.2 Data and Model Poisoning

The evaluation of data and model poisoning, particularly generative backdoors, has historically lacked systematic comparison across model scales, tasks, and triggers [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. To address this fragmentation, recent efforts have introduced unified benchmarking frameworks. In 2024, the introduction of BackdoorLLM established the first comprehensive benchmark for systematically evaluating backdoor threats in open-ended text-generation LLMs [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. 

Testing methodologies in this domain categorize attacks into four paradigms: Data Poisoning Attacks (DPA), Weight Poisoning Attacks (WPA), Chain-of-Thought Attacks (CoTA), and Hidden State Attacks (HSA) [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. The primary evaluation metric is formulated as a trade-off between *clean loss* (the model's ability to maintain normal behavior on benign inputs) and *backdoor loss* (the model's propensity to generate adversary-desired responses when a trigger is present) [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Standardized datasets utilized for these evaluations include Stanford Alpaca, AdvBench, ToxiGen, BOLD, GSM8K, and MATH, which allow researchers to measure the efficacy of backdoors across diverse reasoning and generation tasks [Li_2024_Backdoorllm].

### 7.3 Adversarial Attacks and Red Teaming

Red teaming systematically identifies LLM vulnerabilities through adversarial testing, evolving from manual probing to highly automated frameworks [Wang_2026_LLM]. The standardization of the Attack Success Rate (ASR) has been pivotal in this domain, providing a quantifiable measure of an attack's ability to bypass safety guardrails. Frameworks such as HarmBench provide a standardized environment for automated red teaming evaluation, allowing for consistent comparison of model vulnerabilities [Wang_2026_LLM].

Advanced red teaming methodologies increasingly rely on multi-turn and autonomous agentic interactions. For instance, the MART framework proposes multi-round automatic red teaming for iterative safety improvement, while HARM introduces holistic automated red teaming with top-down test case generation [Wang_2026_LLM]. Furthermore, RedAgent utilizes context-aware autonomous agents to generate jailbreak prompts dynamically [Wang_2026_LLM]. In the context of model alignment, internal red-teaming pipelines are also employed to synthesize high-coverage attack prompts and vulnerable code (e.g., RULE2CODE) specifically for training and supervised fine-tuning, rather than generalized evaluation [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. 

The evaluation of multimodal adversarial attacks introduces additional complexity. Methodologies must account for visual adversarial examples, typographic visual prompt attacks (e.g., FigStep), and compositional adversarial attacks (e.g., Jailbreak in Pieces), which have demonstrated the ability to jailbreak aligned multimodal agents exponentially fast [Wang_2026_LLM].

### 7.4 Prompt Injection

The evaluation of prompt injection vulnerabilities spans both static dataset analysis and dynamic, agentic fuzzing. Static evaluation methodologies emphasize data provenance and rigorous holdout testing. For example, the Mirror benchmark utilizes cryptographic content hashing to ensure that training and evaluation corpora remain strictly disjoint, evaluating linear SVM detectors on a 524-case holdout using F1, precision, and recall metrics [Corll_2026_Mirror]. This approach demonstrates that small, carefully curated models can achieve high recall (e.g., 0.9597) when the data geometry is precisely controlled [Corll_2026_Mirror].

However, static rules often fail to capture the varied nature of indirect prompt injections, necessitating dynamic testing methodologies. Evaluating dynamic, agentic attacks presents unique challenges, primarily due to the sparse, binary feedback signals (success or failure) returned by black-box agents [Wang_2025_LLM]. To overcome this, the AGENTVIGIL framework introduced a generic, automated black-box fuzzing pipeline that utilizes a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) based seed selection algorithm [Wang_2025_LLM]. By employing the Upper Confidence Bound 1 (UCB1) algorithm, AGENTVIGIL balances the exploration of new prompt variants with the exploitation of high-scoring seeds, applying mutation strategies via a helper LLM [Wang_2025_LLM].
